newsitem.title: INDIA: Kashmir leader hopes for talks with separatists.
newsitem.headline: Kashmir leader hopes for talks with separatists.

text.p: be named chief minister of India's Jammu and Kashmir state, said on Wednesday he would beef up a fight against armed militants but hoped to hold talks with separatist leaders.

"We will continue with the security scenario as far as it's concerned, beef it up to meet the challenges," Abdullah told Reuters in New Delhi. His moderate National Conference party swept recent assembly elections in the Himalayan state.
Since the outbreak of the separatist rebellion in 1990, India has deployed tens of thousands of soldiers and paramilitary troops in the region to try to stamp out the insurgency.

"I think we will continue to fight the renegades, the Pakistani infiltrators. This is not only my battle but this is battle of entire nation," said the 62-year-old leader, wearing a traditional Kashmiri kurta-pyjama.
But Abdullah added he hoped to hold talks with leaders of the All Parties Hurriyat (Freedom) Conference, grouping some 30 separatist organisations.
The Hurriyat had called for a boycott of the local polls.

"I hope they (Hurriyat leaders) will come round and we will talk to each other," he said. "Finally we all have to live there. And we would like to bring them round to thinking in terms of the constitution of India....I think dialogue will continue at all levels."
Under the constitution, Jammu and Kashmir state is an integral part of India but enjoys special, autonomous status.

Abdullah refused to participate in national parliamentary elections held earlier this year, saying the Congress government of then prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao was not committed to meeting the autonomy demands.
But after Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda assumed power in June, his centre-left United Front coalition pledged "maximum autonomy" to mostly Hindu India's only Moslem majority state.
Abdullah, traditionally close to Congress, has since veered towards Deve Gowda's centre-left United Front alliance.
"We feel we are part of the United Front government," Farooq said. "Yes, I would join the United Front government."
India's main opposition Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) has opposed moves to grant greater autonomy to Jammu and Kashmir.

"I think we have to convince them (the BJP) that whatever we are going to get, whatever we are going to ask for, is going to be within the constitution of India," Farooq replied when asked about BJP's opposition to his demand for greater autonomy.
He said once the National Conference formed a new government in Srinagar, a committee would be formed to discuss with New Delhi the details of an autonomy package.
Abdullah said Kashmir would need the help of the federal government in Delhi to restore stability in the state.
National Conference officials said they expected Abdullah to be sworn in as chief minister on October 7 or 8.
